title: CFA Ethics 17: Standard I(A) - when local law is looser than the Code of Ethics
subtitle: The rule that picks the stricter side, and the duty to dissociate from a violation
whyItMatters: This is the first Standard and also the most misread: a great many people assume that 'following local law is enough'. For anyone working across borders or in an emerging market, getting this wrong leads straight to a violation.
openingQuestion: You work in a country whose law allows you to take a commission from a third party without disclosing it to the client, while the Code of Ethics requires disclosure. What must you do?
openingOptions: Follow local law, because statute outranks a professional rule in force
Follow the stricter standard - the Code of Ethics
Either, as long as you stay consistent throughout your time in that country
Follow the employer's instruction, since they carry the final legal liability
explanation: Standard I(A) does not say 'comply with the law'. It says comply with the STRICTER of three things: the law where you work, the law where the activity takes place, and the Code of Ethics and Standards. This runs in both directions. If local law forbids what the Code allows, you follow the law. If the Code is stricter than the law, you follow the Code - and this is the direction people skip, because nobody enforces it except CFA Institute itself. The practical consequence: moving to a more lightly regulated market does not lighten your obligations by a single degree.

summary.keyIdea: When local law, the law where the activity happens, and the Code differ, apply the strictest of them - not the nearest one and not the easiest one.
summary.commonMistake: Thinking that complying with local law is enough. The Code is a personal commitment made by the holder of the designation, and it travels with you across every border.

application.title: A situation that comes up often in Vietnam
application.message: An activity that is perfectly lawful under domestic law can still breach the Code. When the two diverge, the answer is always the tighter side.

sections.text: Standard I(A) does not say 'comply with the law'. It says comply with the stricter standard - and that difference is the entire content of this Standard.

items: The law where the activity actually takes place.
The Code of Ethics and the Standards of CFA Institute.

sections.text: The principle runs in both directions. If local law forbids what the Code allows, you follow the law. If the Code is stricter than the law, you follow the Code.

sections.label: The direction people skip
sections.text: The second direction - the Code being stricter than the law - is easy to ignore because no state authority enforces it. The practical consequence: moving to a more lightly regulated market does not lighten your obligations by a single degree.
When you discover a violation around you

The Standard does not require you to report externally. It requires two things: dissociate yourself from the violating conduct, and raise the issue internally through the appropriate channel. The point to remember is that staying silent and carrying on is not a neutral state - it is a form of participation, and it is treated as one.

left.label: Violation
left.text: You sit in an office in market A, where the law does not forbid trading ahead of inside information. The client and the stock are both in market B, where it is forbidden. You trade anyway, arguing that the law where you sit permits it. Wrong on two levels: the law where the activity actually takes place is B's, and independently of that, Standard II(A) forbids this conduct everywhere. When the three sources disagree, the tightest set wins.

right.label: No violation
right.text: The same two markets, except that market A has portfolio-disclosure rules stricter than the Code. You follow A's rules, including for clients in B. Correct - because the principle runs both ways: where the law is stricter than the Code you follow the law, and where the Code is stricter than the law you follow the Code.

sections.label: What dissociating from the conduct means in practice
sections.text: Not staying quiet and continuing to work alongside it. It means the things that leave a trail: refusing to take part in the affected portion of the work, raising the issue in writing through an internal channel, and, if the organisation does not act, considering leaving the role. What the Standard does NOT require is reporting externally - that duty comes from the law of each jurisdiction, not from the Code.

lines: The question is not what the law here permits.
It is which of the three rule sets bearing on you is the tightest.

realWorldExample.description: When you know a colleague or a manager is in violation, Standard I(A) does not require you to report externally - the law in some places even restricts doing so. What it does require is dissociating yourself from the conduct: stop taking part, raise the issue with management or compliance, and if it is not dealt with, consider leaving the role involved. Staying silent and carrying on is a form of participation, even if you were not the one who started it.

quiz.question: Which standard does Standard I(A) require you to apply when the law and the Code conflict?
options: Always the law, since the law is enforceable and the Code is not
Whichever of the law and the Code of Ethics is the stricter
Always the Code, since members pledge to follow it first
The standard of the country where the employer is headquartered
quiz.explanation: The rule runs both ways. Everyone remembers the direction where the law is stricter than the Code; the direction where the Code is stricter than the law is the one that gets skipped. Answering 'always the law' collapses one of those directions, and 'always the Code' collapses the other - both replace a comparison with a fixed winner. Anchoring on the employer's headquarters imports a fourth source the Standard never mentions, and it is the answer that lets a firm choose its own ethics by choosing its address.

quiz.question: How do your obligations change when you move to a market with looser regulation?
options: Heavier, because you must comply with the laws of both countries at once
Lighter, in line with the standard of that new market's rules
It does not lighten, because the Code still binds at its own level
Suspended until membership is re-registered in the new country
quiz.explanation: The Code is a floor that travels with the person, not with the geography. This is what gives Standard I(A) its practical bite for anyone working across borders. The 'lighter' answer is the misreading the Standard exists to correct. 'Heavier' overshoots - the old country's law generally stops applying once the activity moves, though firm policy may not. And nothing is suspended pending re-registration: membership obligations do not pause while paperwork catches up.

quiz.question: When you learn a colleague is in violation, what does Standard I(A) require of you?
options: Wait until real harm has occurred before doing anything
Report it straight to a regulator outside the firm
Document the evidence but carry on working as normal
Dissociate from the conduct and raise it internally
quiz.explanation: The Standard does not require external reporting - in many places the law even restricts it. What it does require is stopping your participation and taking the matter up internally. Waiting for harm gets the timing wrong: the duty attaches on knowledge, not on damage. And documenting while carrying on is the most tempting wrong answer of the four, because it feels responsible - but a record of your discomfort is not dissociation, and the work continuing with your hands on it is exactly what the Standard forbids.

quiz.question: How is carrying on as normal after discovering a violation treated?
options: A form of participation, even if you did not start it
Neutral, since you did not carry out the conduct
Acceptable if you have recorded your disagreement in writing
A breach only if you gain financially from what happened
quiz.explanation: This is the heart of the duty to dissociate: your continued presence lends the conduct legitimacy, whatever you happen to think privately. The 'neutral' answer treats not initiating as the same as not participating. Recording your disagreement is a useful step but not a substitute for stopping. And making it turn on financial gain imports a test from fraud law that the Standard does not use - you can breach it while earning nothing extra at all.

quiz.question: Does Standard I(A) require members to become legal experts?
options: Yes, every member must hold a corresponding licence to practise law
No, but you must understand the law that bears on your own work
No, because legal responsibility rests entirely with the legal team
Yes, and must track every legal change in every country themselves
quiz.explanation: The requirement is a reasonable understanding of the law applying to your own professional activity, and seeking advice when a question goes beyond that - not becoming a lawyer. Both 'yes' options set an impossible bar that no practitioner could meet and that the Standard never states. Delegating everything to the legal department fails in the other direction: you cannot outsource the duty to know enough to recognise when something needs to reach the legal team in the first place.

keyTakeaways: Apply the strictest of the three: the law where you work, the law where the activity happens, and the Code
The 'Code stricter than the law' direction is the one people skip, because nobody enforces it
Moving to a more lightly regulated market does not lighten your obligations
The duty is to dissociate and raise it internally, not to report externally
Staying silent and carrying on is a form of participation

practicePrompt.question: Your firm in country A bans buying or selling shares within 30 days around a report's publication date. You are posted to the branch in country B, where no such rule exists. What should you do?
options: Apply country B's looser rule, because that is where you are now working
Keep the 30-day rule, since it is the stricter of the standards applying to you
Ask the clients which of the two standards they would prefer you to follow
Stop personal investing altogether for the whole period you are in country B
practicePrompt.explanation: Your firm's internal policy and country A's law remain inside the set of standards applying to you, so a change of geography does not remove them. Stopping personal investing entirely is safe but goes beyond what the Standard asks - it demands the strictest of the standards that ACTUALLY apply, not the strictest one imaginable. Asking clients to pick is worse still: an ethical obligation is not something the person you owe it to gets to waive on your behalf.
